title: ‘Money for schools, not war:’ Youth-led protests sweep Europe | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Tens of thousands of young people are slated to fill Europe’s streets on Friday – in an organized international youth-led day of action across more than 25 nations.

Student groups in the UK, France, Spain, Italy and beyond will walk out over the sky-rocketing cost of living, rising tuition fees, underfunded education systems and what they cast as leaders’ complicity in Israel’s war in Gaza.

Other grievances that have promptedGen-Z proteststhis fall include high unemployment, the climate crisis and fears governments are failing to future-proof against unregulated artificial intelligence.

Here’s what you need to know.

Young demonstrators have started to mobilize in central squares and capitals spanning the continent.

Protesters occupiedMilan’s Piazza del Duomo, in northern Italy. Elsewhere, multiple student groups will march in procession toward London’s Parliament Square – at the heart of the British capital.

Up to 10,000 students are expected to participate in rallies in Germany’s western city of Cologne, CNN affiliateRTL Germany reported. Thousands of people have started to march in cities across Italy,according toCNN affiliate Sky TG24, with students in Rome, Genoa, Bologna and Milan calling for an end to rearmament. In Britain alone, students from more than 350 schools, colleges and universities will walk out,according toSocialist Students, one of the groups taking part.

The head of CGIL, Italy’s largest trade union, Maurizio Landini, claimed more than 1 million people will participate in the protests there – though the exact figures are yet to be determined.

“Today is also a ​very important day because young people are taking to the streets not just in Italy but ⁠across Europe,” said Landini, according to Reuters. “The demand for change is growing,” he added.

Ahead of the planned demonstration in Parliament Square, London’s Metropolitan Police said it has been “liaising with organizers.”

“We remain committed to people’s lawful right to protest and free speech, but if behaviour crosses the line into criminality we will take decisive action to uphold the law,” a police spokesperson said in a statement.

Over the past year, Gen Z anti-government protests have touched parts of Europe, theGlobalSouthand theAmericas. Their demands have often evolved as the movements have gathered momentum.

A generation whose adolescence has been marked by the Covid-19 pandemic, climate change and wars in Ukraine, Gaza, Sudan and Iran now fears world leaders are risking their futures by curbing funding for public services in favor of increased military spending. On Friday, protesters in Germany, Italy and Britain voiced concerns over conscription, rising military spending and underfunded public services.

“Young people will not sit quietly while our schools, colleges and universities are cut and billions are found for war,” the national chair of Socialist Students, Adam Powell-Davies, said in a statement. “Fight for our future, not their wars.”

In Italy’s capital, Rome, protesters chanted and held up an array of slogans including“Money for schools, not war,” and “We want to live life without the high cost of living.”

Another lead campaigner, Giorgio Airaudo ofItaly’s CGIL union,described theinternational day of action as a “beautiful day when students, workers and retirees came together to say to no war and rearmament.”

Britain’s Stop the War Coalition, an anti-war advocacy group,echoed callsfor higher wages and greater health care spending – condemning whatthey sawas lawmakers’ “mass rearmament” drive and “complicity with Israel’s genocide.”
